question: How do candles, lamps and soap become industries — and what replaces slaves with palm oil on the African coast?
summary: Light and soap drive this century. Spermaceti, the head matter of the sperm whale, makes the brightest candles, and in 1761 the largest chandlers form a trust to control it ([[ec1]]); American whaling grows into the largest fleet in history, 735 ships, between 1815 and the 1850s ([[ec2]]). Argand's smokeless lamp (1783) and gaslight (1810) make oil a technology of light, then challenge it ([[te1]], [[te2]]). Chevreul's chemistry, Leblanc soda and steam make soap industrial, and consumption doubles ([[th1]], [[te3]], [[ec6]]).

A second chain runs through Africa. When Britain abolishes the slave trade in 1807, British palm-oil imports rise from under 2,000 tons a year in 1815–20 to over 22,000 in 1846–50 ([[o1]], [[ec3]], [[x1]]); the oil is made from natural groves, shipped by Liverpool and Bristol houses that were slave traders, and used for lubricants, candles and soap ([[x3]], [[ec4]], [[ec8]], [[ec7]]). Law argues that this oil boom increased slavery inside West Africa ([[l1]]).

Soap-makers also turn to imported oilseeds as olive oil loses its dominance at Marseille ([[ec5]]), while the olive itself is planted in California ([[x2]]) and the Dutch whale fishery collapses in the revolutionary wars ([[w1]]). Whaling also spreads to the southern hemisphere: Tasmania’s bay whalers make it Australia’s first industry, New Zealand’s shore stations number perhaps a hundred, and by 1795 Yankee whaleships crowd Walvis Bay ([[ec9]], [[ec10]], [[ec11]]). The Pacific ports of Honolulu and Lahaina are the whalers’ base, with six hundred arrivals in 1846, and in Malaya a colonial superintendent plants coconuts and nutmeg ([[ec12]], [[ec13]]). Two smaller fats appear beside them: in Russia the sunflower seed slips past the Orthodox Lenten list of forbidden oils, and cod liver oil is a medicine before anyone knows about vitamins ([[b1]], [[th2]]).

themes.title: The whale's golden age
text: Spermaceti candles, a cartel, and an American fleet at its peak; the Dutch have already gone.

themes.title: Light before electricity
text: From the Argand lamp to gas, light is made by chemistry as much as by fat.

themes.title: Soap becomes industrial
text: Chevreul, Leblanc and steam; consumption doubles; the excise leaves a record; imported oilseeds challenge the olive.

themes.title: From slaves to palm oil
text: Abolition, Biafra's ports, Liverpool and Bristol merchants, the groves, and slavery inside Africa.

themes.title: Palm oil for machines and candles
text: Lubricants for the railways, soap, candles, glycerine and tinplate.

themes.title: Two small fats with large futures
text: The sunflower escapes Russia’s Lenten ban on oils, and cod liver oil is prescribed for rickets and tuberculosis before vitamins are known.

turning_points.text: Argand unveils his lamp in Paris.
Britain abolishes the slave trade; the oil trade fills its place.
Gaslight: a light without a wick.
Chevreul shows what a fat is.

how_to_read: *Economy* has the quantities; *Technology* the lamp, gas and the soap chemistry; *Order* and *Lives* the abolition and its limits.
The Nexus connects the industrial soap chain to the palm-oil boom.

The *picture by region* counts the 26 entries: Europe 15, Far East 1, Africa 4, Americas 3, Oceania 3; none in Near East or Worldwide. It is a British-led story with two edges: African producers and southern-hemisphere whale coasts.

sources.intro: Dolin and Davis et al. for American whaling; Schivelbusch for light; Ward and Lowengard for soap and chemistry; Law, Lynn, Hopkins and Kiple for palm oil.
main: Dolin and Davis, Gallman & Gleiter ([[ec1]], [[ec2]]); Ellis ([[w1]]).
Law, Lynn, Hopkins and Kiple for palm oil ([[o1]], [[ec3]], [[x1]], [[x3]], [[ec4]], [[ec8]], [[ec7]], [[l1]]); Mueller and Kiple for the olive ([[x2]]).
Ellis for the Tasmanian, New Zealand and Namibian whale coasts ([[ec9]], [[ec10]], [[ec11]]).
Dolin for the Hawaiian ports ([[ec12]]); Lees for Penang’s estates ([[ec13]]).
Kiple (Heiser) for the Russian sunflower ([[b1]]); Kiple (O’Keefe) for cod liver oil ([[th2]]).
contested: Dolin gives the fleet's peak as both 1846 and 1854 ([[ec2]]).
Law's argument that the oil boom increased slavery in Africa is a thesis ([[l1]]).
Ward does not name the imported oils that challenged the olive ([[ec5]]).

The Lenten sunflower story is Heiser’s, from Gilmore (1931), with ‘perhaps unknown to the church authorities’ his guess ([[b1]]); cod liver oil’s eighteenth-century medical use is ‘reportedly’ so ([[th2]]).
gaps: Tallow imports from Russia, rapeseed and colza lamp oil, and Marseille’s own records were not read.

India, China and Japan are absent from this folio, and so is the Near East; Oceania appears only as a whale coast, with no Maori or Pacific Islander producer’s voice beyond Ellis’s mention of ‘toungers’.

text: Fifteen entries around Britain, Paris, Marseille and Russia: soap excise and abolition, Chevreul, Argand and gas, Liverpool and Bristol houses, palm oil in Britain, the Dutch whale fishery’s collapse, the Russian sunflower’s Lenten loophole and cod liver oil as a medicine ([[o2]], [[o1]], [[th1]], [[te1]], [[te2]], [[ec4]], [[ec8]], [[ec3]], [[w1]], [[b1]], [[th2]]).
No entry. Nothing in the library covers the Ottoman and Egyptian fats of these years.

One entry: the coconut and nutmeg estates of James Low at Province Wellesley, worked partly by convicts from India ([[ec13]]). Indian, Chinese and Japanese oilseed and whale traditions are otherwise missing from this folio.

The Bight of Biafra becomes the world’s oil coast: the groves, the ports, slavery inside Africa, and Walvis Bay ([[x1]], [[x3]], [[l1]], [[ec11]]). Law, Lynn and Hopkins supply the economic history; African producers are present as an economy, not in their own words.
Spermaceti candles, Nantucket’s fleet and Franciscan olive trees ([[ec1]], [[ec2]], [[x2]]).

Three entries from Ellis and Dolin: Tasmania’s Derwent and New Zealand’s Cook Strait stations, where Maori served as ‘toungers’, and the Hawaiian ports where the Pacific fleet stopped ([[ec9]], [[ec10]], [[ec12]]). These are whaling economies run by Europeans and Americans; nothing in the library records Pacific fats from an islander’s side.
